chapters.title: 7. The Bad Apartment
paragraphs: If on the following morning someone had said to Styopa Likhodeyev, “Styopa! You’ll be shot if you don’t get up this minute!” Styopa would have answered in a languid, barely audible voice, “Shoot me, do whatever you like with me, but I’m not getting up.”

Getting up was out of the question—it seemed to him that he could not even open his eyes, because the moment he did, lightning would flash and his head would instantly be blown to pieces. A heavy bell was booming inside that head, brown spots with fiery green rims were floating between his eyeballs and his closed lids, and to crown it all he felt sick, and it seemed to him that the nausea was somehow connected with the sounds of an insistent gramophone.

Styopa tried to remember something, but only one thing came back to him—that yesterday, apparently, in some unknown place, he had stood with a napkin in his hand and tried to kiss some lady, and had promised her that he would come and visit her the next day, at noon sharp. The lady had declined, saying, “No, no, I won’t be at home!”—but Styopa had stubbornly insisted: “And I’ll just up and come anyway!”

Who the lady was, what time it was now, what day it was and of what month—Styopa had absolutely no idea, and, worst of all, he could not work out where he was. He tried to establish at least the last of these, and to that end he unstuck the gummed-up lids of his left eye. Something was gleaming dully in the half-dark. At last Styopa recognized the pier glass and understood that he was lying on his back in his own bed—that is, in the jeweler’s widow’s former bed—in the bedroom. At this something struck him so hard in the head that he closed the eye and groaned.

Let us explain: Styopa Likhodeyev, director of the Variety Theatre, had come to that morning in his own home, in the very apartment he shared with the late Berlioz, in a large six-story building laid out in a U on Sadovaya Street.

It must be said that this apartment—No. 50—had long enjoyed a reputation that was, if not bad, then at any rate strange. As recently as two years before, its owner had been the widow of the jeweler de Fougeray. Anna Frantsevna de Fougeray, a respectable and very businesslike lady of fifty, let three of its five rooms to lodgers: one, whose name was apparently Belomut, and another whose name has been lost.
And then, two years ago, inexplicable events began in the apartment: people started disappearing from it without a trace.

One day off, a policeman turned up at the apartment, called the second lodger (the one whose name has been lost) out into the hall, and said he was requested to drop by the police station for a minute to sign something. The lodger told Anfisa, Anna Frantsevna’s devoted housekeeper of many years, to say, in case anyone telephoned, that he would be back in ten minutes, and left together with the correct policeman in white gloves. But he did not come back in ten minutes; in fact he never came back at all. Most surprising of all, the policeman had evidently vanished along with him.

The pious—or, to put it more frankly, superstitious—Anfisa told the very upset Anna Frantsevna straight out that this was witchcraft and that she knew perfectly well who had carried off both the lodger and the policeman, only she did not want to say it with night coming on.

Well, witchcraft, as everyone knows, has only to begin, and after that there is no stopping it. The second lodger disappeared, as I recall, on a Monday, and on Wednesday Belomut vanished as if the earth had swallowed him, though under different circumstances, true. In the morning a car called for him as usual to take him to work, and it took him, but it brought no one back and never returned itself.

Madame Belomut’s grief and horror are beyond description. But, alas, neither the one nor the other lasted long. That same night, on returning with Anfisa from the dacha, where for some reason Anna Frantsevna had gone in a hurry, she found Citizen Belomut no longer in the apartment. And that was not all: the doors of both rooms occupied by the Belomut couple turned out to be sealed!
Two days passed somehow or other. On the third day Anna Frantsevna, who had suffered from insomnia all this time, again left in a hurry for the dacha... Need it be said that she did not come back!

Anfisa, left alone, had a good long cry and went to bed after one in the morning. What happened to her after that is not known, but the tenants of other apartments said that knocking of some sort was supposedly heard in No. 50 all night and that the electric light supposedly burned in the windows until morning. In the morning it turned out that Anfisa was gone too!

For a long time all kinds of legends were told in the building about the vanished people and the accursed apartment—for instance, that this dried-up, pious Anfisa supposedly carried on her withered chest, in a little suede bag, twenty-five large diamonds belonging to Anna Frantsevna. That in the woodshed at that very dacha to which Anna Frantsevna had made her hurried trips, some untold treasures had supposedly turned up all by themselves, in the form of those same diamonds, as well as gold coins of tsarist minting... And so on, in the same vein. Well, what we do not know, we cannot vouch for.

Be that as it may, the apartment stood empty and sealed for only a week, and then it was moved into—by the late Berlioz and his wife, and by this same Styopa, also with his wife. Quite naturally, as soon as they got into the accursed apartment, the devil knows what began happening to them too. Namely, within a single month both wives disappeared. But these did not vanish without a trace. Of Berlioz’s wife it was said that she had supposedly been seen in Kharkov with some ballet master, while Styopa’s wife allegedly turned up on Bozhedomka Street, where, so the gossip went, the director of the Variety, using his countless connections, had contrived to get her a room, but on one condition: that there be not a whiff of her on Sadovaya Street...

And so Styopa groaned. He wanted to call the housekeeper Grunya and demand some Pyramidon from her, but he was still able to realize that this was nonsense, that Grunya of course had no Pyramidon. He tried calling Berlioz for help, groaned twice, “Misha... Misha...” but, as you can imagine, got no answer. The apartment was utterly silent.

Wiggling his toes, Styopa guessed that he was lying there in his socks; he ran a trembling hand down his hip to determine whether he had his trousers on or not, and could not determine it. At last, seeing that he was abandoned and alone, that there was no one to help him, he decided to get up, whatever inhuman effort it might cost him.

Styopa unstuck his gummed lids and saw himself reflected in the pier glass as a man with hair sticking out in all directions, with a puffy face covered in black stubble, with swollen eyes, in a dirty shirt with collar and tie, in his underpants and socks.
That was how he saw himself in the pier glass, and next to the mirror he saw an unknown man, dressed in black and wearing a black beret.
Styopa sat up on the bed and goggled his bloodshot eyes at the stranger as far as he could.
It was the stranger who broke the silence, pronouncing the following words in a low, heavy voice with a foreign accent:
“Good day, most charming Stepan Bogdanovich!”
There was a pause, after which, making a terrible effort, Styopa got out:
“What can I do for you?”—and was himself astonished, not recognizing his own voice. He pronounced the word “what” as a treble, “can I” as a bass, and “do for you” did not come out at all.
The stranger smiled amiably, took out a large gold watch with a diamond triangle on the lid, let it chime eleven times, and said:
“Eleven! And it’s exactly an hour that I have been waiting for you to wake up, since you made an appointment with me for ten. Here I am!”
Styopa felt for his trousers on the chair beside the bed and whispered:
“Excuse me...” He put them on and asked hoarsely: “Would you tell me your name, please?”
Speaking was hard for him. With every word someone stuck a needle into his brain, causing him hellish pain.
“What? You’ve forgotten my name too?” At this the stranger smiled.

“Forgive me...” Styopa croaked, feeling that his hangover was presenting him with a new symptom: it seemed to him that the floor beside the bed had gone off somewhere and that any minute now he would fly headfirst to the devil’s mother, down into the underworld.

“My dear Stepan Bogdanovich,” the visitor began, with a shrewd smile, “no Pyramidon will help you. Follow the wise old rule: treat like with like. The only thing that will bring you back to life is two shots of vodka with something sharp and hot to eat.”
Styopa was a cunning man and, ill as he was, realized that since he had been caught in this state, he had better confess everything.
“To be frank,” he began, barely able to move his tongue, “yesterday I had a bit...”
“Not another word!” the visitor replied, and moved off to one side with his armchair.

Styopa, goggling, saw that a tray had been laid on a little table, and on it there was sliced white bread, pressed caviar in a little bowl, pickled porcini mushrooms on a little plate, something in a small saucepan, and, finally, vodka in the jeweler’s widow’s capacious decanter. What particularly struck Styopa was that the decanter was misted with cold. That, however, was understandable—it stood in a slop bowl packed with ice. In a word, the table had been laid neatly and expertly.
The stranger did not allow Styopa’s amazement to develop to a morbid degree and deftly poured him half a shot of vodka.
“And you?” Styopa squeaked.
“With pleasure!”
With a jumping hand Styopa raised the glass to his lips, while the stranger swallowed the contents of his in one gulp. Chewing on a bit of caviar, Styopa squeezed out the words:
“And you... won’t you have a bite?”
“Thank you kindly, I never take a bite,” the stranger replied, and poured a second round. They opened the saucepan—it held frankfurters in tomato sauce.

And then the cursed green before his eyes melted away, words began to come out, and, above all, Styopa remembered something. Namely, that yesterday’s affair had taken place at Skhodnya, at the dacha of the sketch writer Khustov, where this Khustov had taken Styopa in a taxi. He even remembered hiring the taxi outside the Metropol, and there had been some actor or other, or not an actor... with a gramophone in a little suitcase. Yes, yes, yes, it had been at the dacha! And he remembered, too, the dogs howling at that gramophone. Only the lady Styopa had wanted to kiss remained unexplained... the devil knows who she was... she worked in radio, it seemed, or maybe not.

Yesterday, then, was gradually becoming clearer, but just now Styopa was far more interested in today, and in particular in the appearance of a stranger in his bedroom, complete with snacks and vodka. That would be nice to have explained!
“Well, then, I hope you’ve remembered my name now?”
But Styopa only smiled sheepishly and spread his hands.
“Well, really! I sense that after the vodka you drank port! For pity’s sake, how can anyone do that!”
“I’d like to ask you to keep this between us,” Styopa said ingratiatingly.
“Oh, of course, of course! But for Khustov, needless to say, I cannot vouch.”
“You know Khustov, then?”
“Yesterday in your office I caught a glimpse of that individual, but one fleeting look at his face is enough to see that he is a scoundrel, a squabbler, a time-server and a toady.”
“Absolutely right!” thought Styopa, struck by so true, precise and concise a definition of Khustov.

Yes, yesterday was being pieced together from scraps, but the director of the Variety was still uneasy. The point was that there was an enormous black hole gaping in that yesterday. This very stranger in the beret, say what you will, Styopa had certainly not seen in his office yesterday.
“Professor of black magic Woland,” the visitor said weightily, seeing Styopa’s difficulty, and told him everything in order.

Yesterday afternoon he had arrived in Moscow from abroad, immediately come to see Styopa and offered to give performances at the Variety. Styopa had telephoned the Moscow Regional Entertainment Commission and cleared the matter (Styopa turned pale and blinked), signed a contract with Professor Woland for seven performances (Styopa’s mouth fell open), and arranged that Woland would come to him at ten o’clock this morning to settle the details... And so Woland had come. On arrival he had been met by the housekeeper Grunya, who explained that she had only just come in herself, that she did not live in, that Berlioz was not at home, and that if the visitor wished to see Stepan Bogdanovich, he could go into the bedroom himself. Stepan Bogdanovich was sleeping so soundly that she would not undertake to wake him. Seeing the state Stepan Bogdanovich was in, the artiste had sent Grunya to the nearest grocery for vodka and snacks, to the pharmacy for ice and...
“Allow me to settle up with you,” whined the crushed Styopa, and began looking for his wallet.
“Oh, what nonsense!” exclaimed the touring performer, and would not hear another word.

So the vodka and snacks were now explained, and still Styopa was a pitiful sight: he remembered absolutely nothing about a contract and, kill him if you like, had not seen this Woland yesterday. Yes, Khustov had been there, but Woland had not.
“May I have a look at the contract?” Styopa asked quietly.
“Please, please...”

Styopa glanced at the paper and went numb. Everything was in place. First of all, Styopa’s own dashing signature in his own hand! A slanting note in the margin in the handwriting of the financial director Rimsky, authorizing payment to the artiste Woland of ten thousand rubles on account of the thirty-five thousand due to him for seven performances. More than that: right there was Woland’s receipt stating that he had already received these ten thousand!

“What is all this?!” thought the unhappy Styopa, and his head began to spin. Were sinister gaps in his memory starting?! But, it went without saying, now that the contract had been produced, any further expressions of surprise would be simply indecent. Styopa asked his guest’s permission to step out for a minute and, just as he was, in his socks, ran into the front hall to the telephone. On the way he shouted in the direction of the kitchen:
“Grunya!”

But no one answered. Then he glanced at the door of Berlioz’s study, which was next to the front hall, and there, as they say, he was rooted to the spot. On the door handle he made out an enormous wax seal on a cord. “Hello there!” someone barked inside Styopa’s head. “That’s all we needed!” And now Styopa’s thoughts ran along a double track, but, as always happens during a catastrophe, in one direction and, generally, the devil knows where. It is hard even to convey the porridge in Styopa’s head. Here was all that devilry with the black beret, the cold vodka and the incredible contract—and on top of all that, if you please, a seal on the door! I mean, tell anyone you like that Berlioz has been up to something—they won’t believe it, honest to God, they won’t! And yet there was the seal, right there! Yes indeed...

And then some extremely unpleasant little thoughts began to stir in Styopa’s brain about an article that, as luck would have it, he had recently palmed off on Mikhail Alexandrovich for publication in the magazine. And the article, between ourselves, was idiotic! And worthless, and the money was small too...

Immediately after the memory of the article came flying the memory of a certain dubious conversation, which had taken place, as he recalled, on the evening of the twenty-fourth of April, right here in the dining room, when Styopa was having supper with Mikhail Alexandrovich. That is, of course, the conversation could not be called dubious in the full sense of the word (Styopa would never have gone in for such a conversation), but it was a conversation on some unnecessary subject. It would have been perfectly easy, citizens, not to have started it at all. Before the seal, there was no doubt, this conversation could have been considered the merest trifle, but now, after the seal...
“Ah, Berlioz, Berlioz!” it seethed in Styopa’s head. “It just won’t go into my head!”

But there was no time to grieve for long, and Styopa dialed the office of Rimsky, the financial director of the Variety. Styopa’s position was a ticklish one: in the first place, the foreigner might take offense at Styopa checking up on him after the contract had been shown, and in the second, talking to the financial director was extraordinarily difficult. After all, you can hardly ask him outright: “Tell me, did I sign a contract with a professor of black magic for thirty-five thousand rubles yesterday?” That is no way to ask!
“Yes!” came Rimsky’s sharp, unpleasant voice in the receiver.

“Good morning, Grigory Danilovich,” Styopa began quietly. “This is Likhodeyev. The thing is... hm... hm... I have this... er... artiste Woland here with me... So... I wanted to ask, how are things for this evening?..”
“Ah, the black magician?” Rimsky responded in the receiver. “The posters will be ready shortly.”
“Aha,” Styopa said in a weak voice. “Well, bye for now...”
“Will you be in soon?” Rimsky asked.
“In half an hour,” Styopa answered, and, hanging up, clutched his hot head in his hands. Oh, what a nasty business this was turning out to be! What is going on with my memory, citizens? Eh?

It would be awkward, however, to linger in the front hall any longer, and Styopa at once drew up a plan: to conceal his incredible forgetfulness by every means, and now, first of all, to worm out of the foreigner what exactly he intended to show that evening in the Variety entrusted to Styopa’s care.

At this point Styopa turned away from the telephone and, in the mirror that hung in the front hall and had long gone unwiped by the lazy Grunya, distinctly saw some strange individual—long as a pole and wearing a pince-nez (ah, if only Ivan Nikolayevich had been there! He would have recognized this individual at once!). The figure was reflected and immediately vanished. Alarmed, Styopa looked deeper into the hall, and he reeled a second time, for a hefty black cat walked across the mirror and also vanished.
Styopa’s heart sank; he staggered.
“What is all this?” he thought. “Am I going out of my mind? Where are these reflections coming from?!” He looked into the hall and shouted in fright:
“Grunya! What’s this cat hanging around here? Where did it come from? And somebody else as well?!”

“Don’t worry, Stepan Bogdanovich,” a voice responded—not Grunya’s, but the guest’s, from the bedroom. “That cat is mine. Don’t be nervous. And Grunya isn’t here; I’ve sent her off to Voronezh. She complained that you had swindled her out of her holiday.”

These words were so unexpected and absurd that Styopa decided he had misheard. In utter confusion he trotted into the bedroom and froze on the threshold. His hair stirred, and a scattering of fine sweat appeared on his forehead.

The guest was no longer alone in the bedroom but in company. In the second armchair sat the very fellow who had appeared to Styopa in the hall. Now he could be seen clearly: a feathery little mustache, one lens of the pince-nez glinting, and the other lens missing. But there were worse things in the bedroom: lolling in a free-and-easy pose on the jeweler’s widow’s pouf was a third party, namely a black cat of terrifying size, with a shot glass of vodka in one paw and, in the other, a fork on which it had already speared a pickled mushroom.
The light, dim enough in the bedroom as it was, began to fade altogether before Styopa’s eyes. “So this is how people go mad!” he thought, and grabbed hold of the doorpost.
“I see you are a little surprised, my dearest Stepan Bogdanovich?” Woland inquired of Styopa, whose teeth were chattering. “And yet there is nothing to be surprised at. This is my retinue.”
At this the cat drank the vodka, and Styopa’s hand began to slide down the doorpost.
“And this retinue needs room,” Woland went on, “so someone among us here is superfluous in the apartment. And it seems to me that the superfluous one is precisely you!”

“Them, them!” the long checkered one sang out in a goatish voice, speaking of Styopa in the plural. “Generally they’ve been making terrible swine of themselves lately. Boozing, having affairs with women by using their position, not doing a damned thing—and they couldn’t do anything anyway, because they haven’t a clue about the job they’ve been given. Pulling the wool over their superiors’ eyes!”
“Joyriding in the official car!” the cat tattled, chewing a mushroom.
And at this point the fourth and last apparition in the apartment occurred, when Styopa, who had by now slid all the way down to the floor, was scratching at the doorpost with a weakened hand.

Straight out of the pier glass stepped a short but extraordinarily broad-shouldered man, with a bowler hat on his head and a fang sticking out of his mouth that disfigured a physiognomy already unprecedentedly vile. And on top of that, he was fiery red-haired.

“I,” this newcomer joined in the conversation, “generally don’t understand how he ever got to be a director”—the redhead’s nasal twang was growing stronger and stronger—“he’s as much a director as I’m a bishop!”
“You don’t look like a bishop, Azazello,” the cat remarked, helping himself to frankfurters.
“That’s what I’m saying,” twanged the redhead, and, turning to Woland, added respectfully: “Permit me, Messire, to throw him out of Moscow to all the devils?”
“Scat!!” the cat suddenly barked, his fur bristling.
And then the bedroom began spinning around Styopa, and he hit his head on the doorpost and, losing consciousness, thought: “I’m dying...”

But he did not die. Opening his eyes slightly, he saw that he was sitting on something made of stone. Something was making a noise all around him. When he opened his eyes properly, he understood that the noise was the sea, and that, more than that, a wave was rocking at his very feet—that, in short, he was sitting at the very end of a jetty, that above him was a sparkling blue sky, and behind him a white city on the mountains.
Not knowing what one does in such cases, Styopa got up on his trembling legs and walked along the jetty toward the shore.
A man was standing on the jetty, smoking and spitting into the sea. He looked at Styopa with wild eyes and stopped spitting.
Then Styopa pulled the following stunt: he went down on his knees before the unknown smoker and said:
“I beg you, tell me, what city is this?”
“Well, really!” said the heartless smoker.
“I’m not drunk,” Styopa answered hoarsely. “Something has happened to me... I’m ill... Where am I? What city is this?”
“Well, Yalta...”
Styopa sighed quietly, keeled over on his side, and struck his head on the sun-warmed stone of the jetty. Consciousness left him.

chapters.title: 8. The Duel Between the Professor and the Poet
paragraphs: At precisely the time when consciousness left Styopa in Yalta—that is, at about half past eleven in the morning—it returned to Ivan Nikolayevich Bezdomny, who woke after a deep and prolonged sleep. For some time he tried to work out how he had got into an unfamiliar room with white walls, an astonishing night table made of some light-colored metal, and a white blind behind which one could sense the sun.

Ivan shook his head, made sure that it did not ache, and remembered that he was in a hospital. This thought drew after it the memory of Berlioz’s death, but today it did not give Ivan any great shock. Having slept his fill, Ivan Nikolayevich had grown calmer and begun to think more clearly. After lying motionless for a while in the spotlessly clean, soft and comfortable spring bed, Ivan noticed a bell button beside him. Out of a habit of touching things for no reason, Ivan pressed it. He expected some ringing or someone to appear after he pressed the button, but something quite different happened.

At the foot of Ivan’s bed a frosted cylinder lit up, with the word “Drink” written on it. After staying still for a while, the cylinder began to rotate until the word “Nurse” popped up. It goes without saying that the ingenious cylinder astonished Ivan. The word “Nurse” was replaced by the words “Call the doctor.”

“Hm...” said Ivan, not knowing what to do with this cylinder next. But here he had a stroke of luck: Ivan pressed the button a second time at the words “Medical assistant.” The cylinder chimed softly in response, stopped, went out, and into the room came a plump, pleasant woman in a clean white coat, who said to Ivan:
“Good morning!”
Ivan did not answer, considering this greeting inappropriate under the circumstances. Really, they lock a healthy man up in a hospital and then pretend that this is just as it should be!

Meanwhile, without losing her good-natured expression, the woman raised the blind with a single press of a button, and the sun flooded into the room through a light, wide-meshed grille that reached all the way to the floor. Beyond the grille was a balcony, beyond that the bank of a winding river, and on its far bank a cheerful pine wood.
“Please come and take your bath,” the woman invited him, and under her hands an inner wall slid apart, revealing a bathroom and a superbly equipped lavatory.
Although Ivan had decided not to talk to the woman, he could not help himself and, seeing the water gushing into the tub in a broad stream from a gleaming tap, he said ironically:
“Well, look at that! Just like the Metropol!”

“Oh no,” the woman answered proudly, “much better. There’s no equipment like this anywhere, not even abroad. Scientists and doctors come specially to inspect our clinic. We have foreign tourists here every day.”
At the words “foreign tourist” Ivan at once remembered yesterday’s consultant. Ivan’s face clouded; he looked up from under his brows and said:
“Foreign tourists... How you all adore foreign tourists! But there are all sorts among them, by the way. Yesterday, for instance, I met one who was a real treat!”
And he very nearly began telling her about Pontius Pilate, but checked himself, realizing that the woman had no use for such stories and that she could not help him anyway.

Once Ivan Nikolayevich had washed, he was at once issued absolutely everything a man needs after a bath: an ironed shirt, underpants, socks. But that was not all: opening the door of a little wardrobe, the woman pointed inside and asked:
“What would you like to wear—a little robe or some little pajamas?”
Attached to his new dwelling against his will, Ivan very nearly threw up his hands at the woman’s familiarity, and silently jabbed a finger at a pair of crimson flannel pajamas.

After this Ivan Nikolayevich was led down an empty, soundless corridor and brought into an office of the most enormous size. Ivan, having decided to treat everything in this marvelously equipped building with irony, at once christened the office, in his mind, the “factory-kitchen.”

And with good reason. Here stood cabinets and glass cases with gleaming nickel-plated instruments. There were armchairs of extraordinarily complicated design, some pot-bellied lamps with shining shades, a multitude of vials, and gas burners, and electric wires, and instruments completely unknown to anyone.

In the office three people took Ivan in hand—two women and one man, all in white. First of all they took Ivan off to a corner, to a little table, with the evident aim of getting a few things out of him.

Ivan began to think over his situation. Three paths lay before him. The first was extremely tempting: to hurl himself at these lamps and intricate gadgets and smash the lot of them to the devil’s grandmother, and in this way to express his protest at being detained for nothing. But today’s Ivan was already considerably different from yesterday’s Ivan, and the first path seemed doubtful to him: for all he knew, they would become firmly convinced that he was a violent madman. So Ivan rejected the first path. There was a second: to launch at once into the story of the consultant and Pontius Pilate. However, yesterday’s experience showed that this story was not believed or was understood in some perverted way. So Ivan gave up this path as well, deciding to choose the third: to withdraw into proud silence.

He did not manage to carry this out completely and, willy-nilly, he had to answer, though curtly and sullenly, a whole series of questions. And they got absolutely everything out of Ivan about his past life, down to when and how he had had scarlet fever, some fifteen years before. Having filled a whole page with what Ivan told them, they turned it over, and the woman in white moved on to questions about Ivan’s relatives. A tedious rigmarole began: who had died, when, and of what, whether they had drunk, whether they had suffered from venereal diseases, and everything of the sort. In conclusion they asked him to tell about yesterday’s incident at Patriarch’s Ponds, but they did not press him very hard and were not surprised at the information about Pontius Pilate.

Here the woman ceded Ivan to the man, who went at him differently and no longer asked any questions. He took the temperature of Ivan’s body, counted his pulse, and looked into Ivan’s eyes, shining some sort of lamp into them. Then another woman came to the man’s aid, and they pricked Ivan in the back with something, though not painfully, drew some signs on the skin of his chest with the handle of a little hammer, tapped his knees with little hammers, which made Ivan’s legs jump, pricked his finger and took blood from it, pricked him in the crook of his elbow, put some rubber bracelets on his arms...

Ivan only smiled bitterly to himself and reflected on how stupidly and strangely all this had turned out. Just think! He had wanted to warn everyone of the danger posed by the unknown consultant, had meant to catch him, and all he had achieved was to land in some mysterious office in order to tell all sorts of rubbish about Uncle Fyodor, who used to go on drinking binges in Vologda. Unbearably stupid!
At last Ivan was released. He was escorted back to his room, where he was given a cup of coffee, two soft-boiled eggs and white bread with butter.
Having eaten and drunk everything offered, Ivan decided to wait for someone in charge of this institution and from that person in charge to obtain both attention and justice.

And he did get to see him, and very soon after his breakfast. The door to Ivan’s room suddenly opened, and a great many people in white coats came in. At the head of them all walked a man of about forty-five, carefully clean-shaven like an actor, with pleasant but very piercing eyes and courteous manners. His whole retinue showed him marks of attention and respect, and so his entrance came out very solemn. “Like Pontius Pilate!” it occurred to Ivan.
Yes, this was undoubtedly the one in charge. He sat down on a stool, and everyone else remained standing.
“Doctor Stravinsky,” said the seated man, introducing himself to Ivan, and looked at him amiably.
“Here, Alexander Nikolayevich,” someone with a neat little beard said quietly, and handed the man in charge Ivan’s sheet, covered with writing on both sides.

“They’ve stitched together a whole case file!” thought Ivan. And the man in charge ran his practiced eyes over the sheet, muttered “Uh-huh, uh-huh...” and exchanged a few phrases with those around him in a little-known language.

“And he speaks Latin, like Pilate...” Ivan thought sadly. Then one word made him start, and that word was “schizophrenia”—alas, already pronounced yesterday by the accursed foreigner at Patriarch’s Ponds, and repeated here today by Professor Stravinsky.
“And he knew that too!” Ivan thought anxiously.
The man in charge had evidently made it a rule to agree with everything and be pleased with everything, whatever those around him said, and to express this with the words “Splendid, splendid...”
“Splendid!” said Stravinsky, handing the sheet back to someone, and turned to Ivan: “You are a poet?”

“A poet,” Ivan answered gloomily, and for the first time suddenly felt some inexplicable revulsion for poetry, and his own verses, which came back to him at that moment, seemed for some reason unpleasant.
Wrinkling his face, he in turn asked Stravinsky:
“You are a professor?”
To this Stravinsky inclined his head with obliging courtesy.
“And you are in charge here?” Ivan went on.
Stravinsky bowed to this as well.
“I need to talk to you,” Ivan Nikolayevich said significantly.
“That is what I’ve come for,” Stravinsky responded.
“The thing is this,” Ivan began, feeling that his hour had come. “They’ve dressed me up as a madman, nobody wants to listen to me!..”
“Oh no, we will hear you out very attentively,” Stravinsky said seriously and soothingly, “and we will by no means allow you to be dressed up as a madman.”

“Then listen: yesterday evening at Patriarch’s Ponds I met a mysterious individual, a foreigner or maybe not a foreigner, who knew in advance about Berlioz’s death and had personally seen Pontius Pilate.”
The retinue listened to the poet silently and without stirring.
“Pilate? Pilate—that’s the one who lived in the time of Jesus Christ?” Stravinsky asked, squinting at Ivan.
“The very same.”
“Aha,” said Stravinsky, “and this Berlioz died under a tram?”
“That’s exactly who got cut down by a tram yesterday at Patriarch’s, right in front of me, and this same mysterious citizen...”
“The acquaintance of Pontius Pilate?” asked Stravinsky, who was evidently distinguished by great quickness of understanding.

“Him exactly,” Ivan confirmed, studying Stravinsky. “Well, he said in advance that Annushka had spilled the sunflower oil... And he slipped right on that very spot! What do you make of that?” Ivan inquired significantly, hoping to produce a great effect with his words.
But no such effect followed, and Stravinsky quite simply asked the next question:
“And who is this Annushka?”
This question upset Ivan a little; his face twitched.

“Annushka is completely unimportant here,” he said nervously. “The devil knows who she is. Just some fool from Sadovaya. What’s important is that he knew about the sunflower oil in advance, you understand, in advance! Do you understand me?”
“Perfectly,” Stravinsky answered seriously and, touching the poet’s knee, added: “Don’t get upset, and go on.”

“I’m going on,” said Ivan, trying to match Stravinsky’s tone and knowing from bitter experience by now that only calm would help him. “So, this terrible character—and he’s lying when he says he’s a consultant—possesses some kind of extraordinary power... For instance, you chase after him, and there’s no way to catch him. And there’s a pair with him, and they’re a fine pair too, in their own way: some lanky one in broken glasses and, besides him, a cat of incredible size who rides the tram on his own. Besides that”—with no one interrupting him, Ivan spoke with ever greater heat and conviction—“he was personally on Pontius Pilate’s balcony, there’s no doubt about it whatsoever. What is all this, then? Eh? He has to be arrested immediately, or he’ll do indescribable harm.”
“So what you’re trying to achieve is to have him arrested? Have I understood you correctly?” asked Stravinsky.
“He’s clever,” thought Ivan. “I have to admit that among the intelligentsia, too, you come across some rarely clever ones. There’s no denying it.” And he answered:

“Perfectly correctly! And how could I not, just think about it yourself! And meanwhile I’m being held here by force, they poke a lamp in my eyes, bathe me in a tub, ask me things about Uncle Fedya!.. And he’s been dead for ages! I demand to be released immediately.”

“Well then, splendid, splendid!” Stravinsky responded. “Now everything is clear. Indeed, what sense is there in keeping a healthy man in the hospital? Very well, sir. I will discharge you from here at once if you tell me that you are normal. Not prove it, only tell me. So, are you normal?”
At this a complete silence fell, and the fat woman who had looked after Ivan that morning gazed reverently at the professor, while Ivan thought once again: “Positively clever.”
He liked the professor’s offer very much; however, before answering, he thought very, very hard, wrinkling his forehead, and at last said firmly:
“I am normal.”

“Well, that’s splendid,” Stravinsky exclaimed with relief, “and if so, then let us reason logically. Let us take your day yesterday”—here he turned, and Ivan’s sheet was immediately handed to him. “In search of an unknown man who introduced himself to you as an acquaintance of Pontius Pilate, yesterday you performed the following actions”—here Stravinsky began bending down his long fingers, glancing now at the sheet, now at Ivan—“you hung a little icon on your chest. Did you?”
“I did,” Ivan agreed sullenly.

“You fell off a fence and injured your face. Right? You turned up at a restaurant with a lighted candle in your hand, in nothing but your underwear, and in the restaurant you beat somebody. You were brought here tied up. Once here, you telephoned the police and asked them to send machine guns. Then you made an attempt to throw yourself out of the window. Right? The question is: is it possible, acting in this way, to catch or arrest anyone? And if you are a normal man, you will answer yourself: by no means. You wish to leave here? By all means, sir. But allow me to ask you, where will you go?”
“To the police, of course,” Ivan answered, no longer so firmly and a little flustered under the professor’s gaze.
“Directly from here?”
“Uh-huh.”
“And you won’t stop at your apartment?” Stravinsky asked quickly.
“There’s no time to be stopping anywhere! While I’m running around to apartments, he’ll slip away!”
“I see. And what will you tell the police first of all?”
“About Pontius Pilate,” Ivan Nikolayevich answered, and his eyes clouded with a somber haze.

“Well, that’s splendid!” exclaimed the conquered Stravinsky and, turning to the one with the little beard, ordered: “Fyodor Vasilyevich, please discharge Citizen Bezdomny to town. But don’t let this room be taken, and the bed linen needn’t be changed. In two hours Citizen Bezdomny will be here again. Well then,” he turned to the poet, “I will not wish you success, because I don’t believe in that success one iota. See you soon!” And he stood up, and his retinue stirred.
“On what grounds will I be here again?” Ivan asked anxiously.
Stravinsky seemed to have been waiting for this question; he immediately sat down again and began to speak:

“On the grounds that as soon as you turn up at the police in your underpants and say that you have met a man who personally knew Pontius Pilate, you will instantly be brought back here, and you will find yourself again in this very same room.”
“What have underpants got to do with it?” Ivan asked, looking around in bewilderment.

“Mainly Pontius Pilate. But underpants as well. We will take the hospital linen off you, after all, and give you back your own clothes. And you were delivered to us in your underpants. And meanwhile you had no intention whatsoever of stopping at your apartment, even though I hinted at it to you. Next will come Pilate... and that’s that!”
At this something strange happened to Ivan Nikolayevich. His will seemed to split, and he felt that he was weak, that he needed advice.
“So what should I do?” he asked, timidly this time.

“Well, that’s splendid!” Stravinsky responded. “That is a most reasonable question. Now I will tell you what has actually happened to you. Yesterday someone badly frightened and upset you with a story about Pontius Pilate and other things. And so you, a nervous, overwrought man, went around the city telling people about Pontius Pilate. It is perfectly natural that they take you for a madman. Your salvation now lies in only one thing—complete rest. And you absolutely must stay here.”
“But he has to be caught!” Ivan exclaimed, imploringly now.

“Very well, sir, but why should you run around yourself? Set down on paper all your suspicions and accusations against this man. Nothing could be simpler than to forward your statement to the proper quarter, and if, as you suppose, we are dealing with a criminal, all this will be cleared up very soon. But just one condition: don’t strain your head, and try to think less about Pontius Pilate. People can tell all sorts of things! One needn’t believe everything.”
“I understand!” Ivan declared resolutely. “Please issue me paper and a pen.”
“Issue him paper and a short pencil,” Stravinsky ordered the fat woman, and to Ivan he said: “But I advise you not to write today.”
“No, no, today, definitely today,” Ivan cried in alarm.
“Very well. Only don’t strain your brain. If it doesn’t work out today, it will tomorrow.”
“He’ll get away!”

“Oh no,” Stravinsky objected confidently, “he won’t get away anywhere, I guarantee you. And remember that here you will be helped in every possible way, and without that nothing will come of it for you. Do you hear me?” Stravinsky suddenly asked significantly, and took possession of both of Ivan Nikolayevich’s hands. Holding them in his own, he looked Ivan straight in the eyes for a long time and repeated: “You will be helped here... do you hear me?.. You will be helped here... You will get relief. It is quiet here, everything is calm... You will be helped here...”
Ivan Nikolayevich unexpectedly yawned, and the expression of his face softened.
“Yes, yes,” he said quietly.

“Well, that’s splendid!” Stravinsky concluded the conversation, as was his custom, and rose. “Goodbye!” He shook Ivan’s hand and, on his way out, turned to the one with the little beard and said: “Yes, and try oxygen... and baths.”

A few moments later neither Stravinsky nor his retinue was before Ivan any longer. Beyond the mesh in the window, in the noon sun, the joyful spring wood on the far bank stood in all its beauty, and nearer by the river sparkled.

chapters.title: 9. Koroviev’s Tricks
paragraphs: Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy, chairman of the tenants’ association of building No. 302-bis on Sadovaya Street in Moscow, where the late Berlioz had lived, had been in the most terrible bother ever since the previous night, from Wednesday to Thursday.
At midnight, as we already know, a commission that included Zheldybin had arrived at the building, summoned Nikanor Ivanovich, informed him of Berlioz’s death, and gone with him to apartment No. 50.

There the manuscripts and belongings of the deceased were placed under seal. Neither Grunya, the daily housekeeper, nor the frivolous Stepan Bogdanovich was in the apartment at the time. The commission informed Nikanor Ivanovich that it would take the manuscripts of the deceased to sort through them, that his living space, that is, three rooms (the jeweler’s widow’s former study, drawing room and dining room), would pass into the hands of the tenants’ association, and that his belongings were to be kept in the said space until the heirs were announced.

The news of Berlioz’s death spread through the whole building with a sort of supernatural speed, and from seven o’clock on Thursday morning people began telephoning Bosoy, and then turning up in person, with applications containing claims to the deceased’s living space. And within two hours Nikanor Ivanovich had received thirty-two such applications.

They contained pleas, threats, slanders, denunciations, promises to carry out repairs at the applicant’s own expense, references to unbearably cramped conditions and to the impossibility of living in one apartment with bandits. Among other things there was a description, staggering in its artistic power, of the theft of some pelmeni, packed directly into a jacket pocket, in apartment No. 31, two promises to commit suicide and one confession of a secret pregnancy.
Nikanor Ivanovich was called out into the front hall of his apartment, taken by the sleeve, whispered to, winked at and promised that his kindness would not go unrewarded.

This torment went on until shortly after noon, when Nikanor Ivanovich simply fled from his apartment to the management office by the gate, but when he saw that they were lying in wait for him there too, he fled from there as well. Having somehow beaten off those who followed hard on his heels across the asphalt courtyard, Nikanor Ivanovich vanished into the sixth entrance and went up to the fifth floor, where that vile apartment No. 50 was located.

After catching his breath on the landing, the corpulent Nikanor Ivanovich rang, but no one opened. He rang again and again and began to grumble and curse quietly. But even then no one opened. Nikanor Ivanovich’s patience snapped, and, taking out of his pocket a bunch of duplicate keys belonging to the building management, he opened the door with an authoritative hand and went in.
“Hey, housekeeper!” Nikanor Ivanovich shouted in the half-dark front hall. “What’s your name? Grunya, is it? You not here?”
No one answered.

Then Nikanor Ivanovich took a folding rule out of his briefcase, freed the study door of its seal, and stepped into the study. Step in he did, but he stopped in the doorway in amazement and even gave a start.
At the deceased’s desk sat an unknown, skinny, long citizen in a little checkered jacket, a little jockey cap and a pince-nez... well, in a word, that very one.
“And who might you be, citizen?” Nikanor Ivanovich asked in fright.

“Well, well! Nikanor Ivanovich!” yelled the unexpected citizen in a jangling tenor and, jumping up, greeted the chairman with a forcible and sudden handshake. This greeting did not gladden Nikanor Ivanovich in the least.
“Begging your pardon,” he began suspiciously, “who might you be? Are you an official person?”

“Ah, Nikanor Ivanovich!” the stranger exclaimed with feeling. “What is an official person or an unofficial one? It all depends on the point of view from which you look at the matter. It’s all shaky and relative, Nikanor Ivanovich. Today I’m an unofficial person, and tomorrow, before you know it, I’m an official one! And it happens the other way round too, and how it happens!”

This line of reasoning did not satisfy the chairman of the building management to any degree. Being by nature a generally suspicious man, he concluded that the citizen holding forth before him was precisely an unofficial person, and very likely an idle one too.
“But who might you be? What’s your name?” the chairman asked more and more sternly, and even began advancing on the stranger.
“My name,” the citizen responded, not in the least put out by the sternness, “is, well, let’s say Koroviev. But won’t you have a bite to eat, Nikanor Ivanovich? No ceremony! Eh?”

“Begging your pardon,” Nikanor Ivanovich began, indignant by now, “what bites to eat are we talking about!” (It must be admitted, unpleasant as it is, that Nikanor Ivanovich was somewhat crude by nature.) “Sitting in the deceased’s half is not permitted! What are you doing here?”
“Do sit down, Nikanor Ivanovich,” the citizen yelled, not in the least disconcerted, and began fussing around, offering the chairman an armchair.
Completely infuriated, Nikanor Ivanovich rejected the armchair and bawled:
“But who are you?”

“I, if you please, serve as interpreter to the person of a foreigner who has taken up residence in this apartment,” the man who had called himself Koroviev introduced himself, and clicked the heel of his unpolished reddish-brown shoe.
Nikanor Ivanovich’s mouth fell open. The presence of some foreigner in this apartment, and with an interpreter at that, came as a complete surprise to him, and he demanded explanations.

The interpreter willingly explained. The foreign artiste Mr. Woland had been kindly invited by the director of the Variety, Stepan Bogdanovich Likhodeyev, to spend the time of his engagement, a week or so, in his apartment, which he had written to Nikanor Ivanovich about only yesterday, with a request to register the foreigner temporarily while Likhodeyev himself took a trip to Yalta.
“He never wrote me anything,” the chairman said in amazement.
“Just have a rummage in your briefcase, Nikanor Ivanovich,” Koroviev suggested sweetly.
Nikanor Ivanovich, shrugging, opened his briefcase and found Likhodeyev’s letter in it.
“How could I have forgotten about it?” Nikanor Ivanovich muttered, staring dully at the opened envelope.

“That’s nothing, worse things happen, Nikanor Ivanovich!” Koroviev rattled on. “Absent-mindedness, absent-mindedness, and overwork, and high blood pressure, our dear friend Nikanor Ivanovich! I’m terribly absent-minded myself. Some time over a glass I’ll tell you a few facts from my biography—you’ll die laughing!”
“But when is Likhodeyev going to Yalta?!”

“Why, he’s gone already, gone!” cried the interpreter. “He’s already rolling along, you know! He’s already the devil knows where!” And here the interpreter waved his arms like the sails of a windmill.
Nikanor Ivanovich declared that he absolutely had to see the foreigner in person, but the interpreter turned him down: quite impossible. Busy. Training the cat.
“The cat, if you like, I can show you,” Koroviev offered.
This in turn Nikanor Ivanovich declined, whereupon the interpreter at once made the chairman an unexpected but highly interesting proposal.

Since Mr. Woland would not hear of living in a hotel, and he was used to living spaciously, wouldn’t the tenants’ association rent him, for a week or so, while Woland’s engagement in Moscow lasted, the whole apartment, that is, the deceased’s rooms as well?
“After all, it’s all the same to him, the deceased,” Koroviev wheezed in a whisper. “You’ll agree yourself, Nikanor Ivanovich, he’s no use for this apartment now, is he?”
Nikanor Ivanovich, somewhat bewildered, objected that foreigners were supposed to live at the Metropol, and not at all in private apartments...

“I tell you, he’s as capricious as the devil knows what!” Koroviev whispered. “He just doesn’t want to! He doesn’t like hotels! I’ve had them up to here, these foreign tourists!” Koroviev complained confidentially, jabbing a finger at his sinewy neck. “Believe me, they’ve worn my soul out! One of them comes... and either he spies like the worst son of a bitch or he wears you out with his whims: this isn’t right and that isn’t right!.. But for your association, Nikanor Ivanovich, it’s the most complete gain and an obvious profit. And he won’t haggle over money.” Koroviev glanced around and then whispered in the chairman’s ear: “A millionaire!”

There was clear practical sense in the interpreter’s proposal; the proposal was very solid, but there was something remarkably unsolid both in the interpreter’s manner of speaking and in his clothes, and in that loathsome, good-for-nothing pince-nez. Because of this, something vague weighed on the chairman’s soul, and still he decided to accept the proposal. The point was that the tenants’ association had, alas, a very sizable deficit. By autumn they would have to buy oil for the steam heating, and with what dough—nobody knew. But with the foreign tourist’s money they could perhaps scrape through. But the businesslike and cautious Nikanor Ivanovich declared that first of all he would have to coordinate this question with the Intourist bureau.

“I understand!” cried Koroviev. “Of course it has to be coordinated! Absolutely! Here’s the telephone, Nikanor Ivanovich, coordinate away this minute! And don’t be shy about the money,” he added in a whisper, drawing the chairman into the front hall to the telephone, “who else should you take it from, if not from him! If you could see the villa he has in Nice! Next summer, when you go abroad, drop in on purpose to have a look—you’ll gasp!”

The matter with the Intourist bureau was settled over the telephone with an extraordinary speed that astonished the chairman. It turned out that they already knew there of Mr. Woland’s intention to live in Likhodeyev’s private apartment and had no objection to it whatsoever.
“Well, that’s marvelous!” yelled Koroviev.

Somewhat stunned by his chatter, the chairman declared that the tenants’ association agreed to let apartment No. 50 to the artiste Woland for a week at a rate of... Nikanor Ivanovich faltered a little and said:
“Five hundred rubles a day.”
At this Koroviev utterly astonished the chairman. Winking thievishly in the direction of the bedroom, from which came the soft thuds of a heavy cat jumping, he wheezed:
“So for a week that comes to three and a half thousand?”
Nikanor Ivanovich thought he would add to this: “Well, you’ve got some appetite, Nikanor Ivanovich!” But Koroviev said something quite different:
“Why, is that a sum? Ask for five, he’ll give it.”

With a bewildered grin, Nikanor Ivanovich, without himself noticing how, found himself at the deceased’s desk, where Koroviev, with the greatest speed and dexterity, drew up a contract in two copies. After this he flew off with it into the bedroom and came back, and both copies had already been signed by the foreigner with a sweeping hand. The chairman signed the contract too. Then Koroviev asked for a little receipt for five...

“In words, in words, Nikanor Ivanovich!.. thousand rubles...” And with words that somehow did not suit a serious matter—“Ein, zwei, drei!”—he laid out before the chairman five brand-new bank-wrapped bundles.
A count took place, sprinkled with Koroviev’s little jokes and sayings, such as “money loves to be counted,” “your own eye is your best watchman” and others of the same sort.

Having counted the money, the chairman received from Koroviev the foreigner’s passport for temporary registration, put it, the contract and the money into his briefcase and, somehow unable to restrain himself, bashfully asked for a little free pass...
“Don’t mention it!” roared Koroviev. “How many tickets would you like, Nikanor Ivanovich, twelve, fifteen?”
The stunned chairman explained that he needed only a couple of passes, for himself and Pelageya Antonovna, his wife.

Koroviev at once whipped out a notepad and dashingly wrote out for Nikanor Ivanovich a little pass for two persons in the front row. And this little pass the interpreter deftly slipped to Nikanor Ivanovich with his left hand, while with his right he put into the chairman’s other hand a thick, crackling bundle. Darting a glance at it, Nikanor Ivanovich turned deep red and began pushing it away from himself.
“That’s not done...” he muttered.
“I won’t hear of it,” Koroviev whispered right into his ear. “With us it’s not done, but with foreigners it is. You’ll offend him, Nikanor Ivanovich, and that would be awkward. You’ve put in work...”
“It’s severely prosecuted,” the chairman whispered very, very quietly, and glanced around.
“And where are the witnesses?” Koroviev whispered into his other ear. “I ask you, where are they? What’s the matter with you?”

And then, as the chairman later maintained, a miracle occurred: the bundle crawled into his briefcase by itself. And then the chairman, feeling somehow limp and even broken, found himself on the stairs. A whirlwind of thoughts raged in his head. Spinning around in it were that villa in Nice, and the trained cat, and the thought that there really had been no witnesses, and that Pelageya Antonovna would be pleased with the pass. These were disconnected thoughts, but on the whole pleasant ones. And nevertheless, somewhere at the very bottom of his soul, a little needle was pricking the chairman. It was the little needle of anxiety. Moreover, right there on the stairs, a thought struck the chairman like a blow: “But how did the interpreter get into the study if there was a seal on the door?! And how is it that he, Nikanor Ivanovich, didn’t ask about it?” For some time the chairman stared at the steps like a ram, but then he decided to spit on it and not torment himself with an intricate question...
As soon as the chairman had left the apartment, a low voice came from the bedroom:
“I didn’t like this Nikanor Ivanovich. He is a grasping rogue and a cheat. Couldn’t it be arranged so that he doesn’t come here again?”
“Messire, you have only to command it!..” Koroviev responded from somewhere, not in a jangling voice but in a very clear and resonant one.
And at once the accursed interpreter turned up in the front hall, dialed a number and for some reason began speaking into the receiver very tearfully:

“Hello! I consider it my duty to report that the chairman of our tenants’ association of building number three hundred and two-bis on Sadovaya, Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy, is speculating in foreign currency. At this very moment, in his apartment number thirty-five, in the ventilation duct, in the lavatory, wrapped in newspaper, there are four hundred dollars. This is a resident of the said building, from apartment number eleven, Timofei Kvastsov, speaking. But I beseech you to keep my name secret. I fear the revenge of the above-stated chairman.”
And he hung up, the scoundrel!

What happened next in apartment No. 50 is not known, but it is known what happened at Nikanor Ivanovich’s. Having locked himself in his lavatory on the hook, he pulled out of his briefcase the bundle that the interpreter had forced on him and made sure that it contained four hundred rubles. Nikanor Ivanovich wrapped this bundle in a scrap of newspaper and stuck it into the ventilation duct.

Five minutes later the chairman was sitting at the table in his small dining room. His wife brought from the kitchen some neatly sliced herring, thickly sprinkled with green onion. Nikanor Ivanovich poured himself a small glass of vodka, drank it, poured a second, drank it, speared three pieces of herring on his fork... and at that moment the doorbell rang. And Pelageya Antonovna carried in a steaming saucepan, one look at which told you at once that in it, amid the thick of a fiery borscht, was the most delicious thing in the world—a marrowbone.
Swallowing his saliva, Nikanor Ivanovich growled like a dog:
“Damn you all to perdition! They won’t let a man eat. Don’t let anybody in, I’m not here, not here. About the apartment, tell them to stop yapping. There’ll be a meeting in a week...”

His wife ran into the front hall, and Nikanor Ivanovich, with a ladle, hauled it out of the fire-breathing lake—it, the bone, cracked lengthwise. And at that moment two citizens came into the dining room, and with them, for some reason, a very pale Pelageya Antonovna. At the sight of the citizens Nikanor Ivanovich turned white too, and rose.
“Where’s the john?” asked the first, the one in the white Russian blouse, in a preoccupied way.
Something knocked on the dinner table (it was Nikanor Ivanovich dropping his ladle on the oilcloth).
“Here, here,” Pelageya Antonovna answered in a patter.
And the visitors immediately rushed into the corridor.
“What’s this about?” Nikanor Ivanovich asked quietly, following the visitors. “We can’t have anything like that in our apartment... And your little documents... begging your pardon...”

The first, without stopping, showed Nikanor Ivanovich a little document, and in that same minute the second was found standing on a stool in the lavatory, with his arm thrust into the ventilation duct. Everything went dark before Nikanor Ivanovich’s eyes. They took off the newspaper, but the bundle turned out to contain not rubles but some unknown money, sort of blue, sort of green, with pictures of some old man. However, Nikanor Ivanovich did not see all this clearly; some sort of spots were floating before his eyes.
“Dollars in the ventilation duct,” the first said thoughtfully, and asked Nikanor Ivanovich gently and politely: “Your little packet?”
“No!” Nikanor Ivanovich answered in a terrible voice. “Enemies planted it!”
“That happens,” the first one agreed, and again added gently: “Well, then, you’ll have to hand over the rest.”
“I haven’t got any! I haven’t, I swear to God, I’ve never held any in my hands!” the chairman cried desperately.
He rushed to the chest of drawers, pulled out a drawer with a crash, and out of it his briefcase, crying out incoherently as he did so:
“Here’s the contract... that viper of an interpreter planted it... Koroviev... in a pince-nez!”

He opened the briefcase, glanced into it, thrust his hand into it, turned blue in the face and dropped the briefcase into the borscht. There was nothing in the briefcase: no letter from Styopa, no contract, no foreigner’s passport, no money, no free pass. In a word, nothing except the folding rule.
“Comrades!” the chairman shouted frantically. “Hold them! There are unclean powers in our building!”
And here the devil knows what Pelageya Antonovna imagined, but she threw up her hands and cried:
“Confess, Ivanych! They’ll go easier on you!”
With bloodshot eyes, Nikanor Ivanovich raised his fists over his wife’s head, wheezing:
“Ugh, you damned fool!”
At this he grew weak and sank onto a chair, evidently having decided to submit to the inevitable.
Meanwhile, out on the landing, Timofei Kondratyevich Kvastsov was pressing now his ear, now his eye to the keyhole of the chairman’s apartment door, languishing with curiosity.

Five minutes later the residents of the building who were out in the courtyard saw the chairman, accompanied by two other persons, proceed straight to the gates of the building. They said that Nikanor Ivanovich looked like death, that he was swaying as he walked, like a drunk, and was muttering something.

And an hour after that an unknown citizen turned up at apartment No. 11, just at the moment when Timofei Kondratyevich was telling the other tenants, choking with delight, how the chairman had been nabbed; he beckoned Timofei Kondratyevich out of the kitchen into the front hall with his finger, said something to him, and vanished together with him.

chapters.title: 10. News from Yalta
paragraphs: At the time when misfortune befell Nikanor Ivanovich, not far from building No. 302-bis, on the same Sadovaya, two people were in the office of Rimsky, the financial director of the Variety: Rimsky himself and the Variety’s house manager, Varenukha.

The large office on the theater’s second floor looked out with two windows onto Sadovaya, and with one, right behind the back of the financial director as he sat at his desk, onto the Variety’s summer garden, where there were refreshment bars, a shooting gallery and an open-air stage. The furnishings of the office, apart from the desk, consisted of a bundle of old posters hanging on the wall, a little table with a carafe of water, four armchairs, and a stand in the corner on which stood a dusty model of some revue from long ago. Well, it goes without saying that, besides all this, there was in the office a small, battered, peeling fireproof safe, to Rimsky’s left, next to the desk.

Rimsky, sitting at his desk, had been in a bad mood since early morning, whereas Varenukha, by contrast, was very lively and somehow especially restless in his activity. And yet there was no outlet for his energy.
Varenukha was hiding just now in the financial director’s office from the free-pass seekers, who poisoned his life, especially on days when the program changed. And today was just such a day.
The moment the telephone began to ring, Varenukha would pick up the receiver and lie into it:
“Who? Varenukha? He’s not here. He’s left the theater.”
“Call Likhodeyev once more, will you, please,” Rimsky said irritably.
“But he isn’t at home. I already sent Karpov. There’s nobody in the apartment.”
“The devil knows what this is,” Rimsky hissed, clicking away at the adding machine.
The door opened, and an usher dragged in a thick bundle of freshly printed supplementary posters. On the green sheets, in large red letters, was printed:
TODAY AND DAILY AT THE VARIETY THEATRE
IN ADDITION TO THE PROGRAM:
PROFESSOR WOLAND
SESSIONS OF BLACK MAGIC WITH ITS COMPLETE EXPOSURE
Varenukha, stepping back from the poster, which he had thrown over the model, admired it and ordered the usher to send all the copies out to be pasted up at once.
“Good, eye-catching,” Varenukha remarked when the usher had gone.
“And I dislike this undertaking in the extreme,” Rimsky grumbled, glancing spitefully at the poster through his horn-rimmed glasses, “and in general I’m surprised they allowed him to put it on!”
“No, Grigory Danilovich, don’t say that, it’s a very subtle move. The whole point is in the exposure.”

“I don’t know, I don’t know, there’s no point in it at all, and he’s always cooking up something like this! If only he’d shown us this magician. Have you seen him? Where he dug him up, the devil knows!”

It turned out that Varenukha, like Rimsky, had not seen the magician. Yesterday Styopa (“like a madman,” as Rimsky put it) had come running to the financial director with a draft of the contract already written, ordered it to be copied out on the spot and the money paid. And this magician had cleared off, and no one had seen him except Styopa himself.

Rimsky took out his watch, saw that it showed five past two, and became absolutely furious. Really! Likhodeyev had called at about eleven o’clock, said he would be there in half an hour, and not only had he not come, he had vanished from his apartment too!
“My work is at a standstill!” Rimsky was growling now, jabbing a finger at a pile of unsigned papers.
“Couldn’t he have fallen under a tram, like Berlioz?” Varenukha was saying, holding to his ear a receiver in which thick, prolonged and completely hopeless signals could be heard.
“And a good thing it would be...” Rimsky said through his teeth, barely audibly.

At that very moment a woman came into the office in a uniform jacket, a cap, a black skirt and canvas slippers. From a little pouch on her belt the woman took out a small white square and a notebook and asked:
“Where’s the Variety here? Extra-urgent telegram for you. Sign.”
Varenukha scrawled some squiggle in the woman’s notebook and, as soon as the door had banged shut behind her, opened the square.
Having read the telegram, he blinked and handed the square to Rimsky.

The following was printed in the telegram: “Yalta to Moscow Variety Today half past eleven criminal investigation visited by brown-haired man nightshirt trousers no boots mental case called himself Likhodeyev director Variety Wire urgently Yalta investigation where director Likhodeyev.”
“Well, hello, I’m your auntie!” Rimsky exclaimed, and added: “Another surprise!”

“A False Dmitry,” said Varenukha, and began speaking into the telephone receiver: “Telegraph office? Variety account. Take an extra-urgent telegram... Are you listening?.. ‘Yalta criminal investigation... Director Likhodeyev in Moscow Financial director Rimsky’...”
Regardless of the report about the Yalta impostor, Varenukha again set about searching for Styopa by telephone wherever he could and, naturally, found him nowhere.

Just when Varenukha, holding the receiver in his hands, was wondering where else he might call, in came the same woman who had brought the first urgent telegram, and handed Varenukha a new little envelope. Tearing it open in haste, Varenukha read what was printed and whistled.
“What now?” Rimsky asked, with a nervous jerk.

Varenukha silently handed him the telegram, and the financial director saw in it the words: “Beg you believe thrown to Yalta by Woland hypnosis wire urgently criminal investigation confirmation identity Likhodeyev.”
Rimsky and Varenukha, their heads touching, reread the telegram, and having reread it, stared at each other in silence.
“Citizens!” the woman suddenly grew angry. “Sign first, and then you can be silent as long as you like! I deliver urgent telegrams, you know.”
Varenukha, without taking his eyes off the telegram, signed crookedly in the notebook, and the woman disappeared.
“But you talked to him on the phone just after eleven, didn’t you?” the house manager began in complete bewilderment.
“It’s ridiculous to even talk about it!” Rimsky shouted piercingly. “Talked or didn’t talk, he can’t be in Yalta now! It’s ridiculous!”
“He’s drunk...” said Varenukha.
“Who’s drunk?” asked Rimsky, and again they both stared at each other.

That some impostor or madman was telegraphing from Yalta there was no doubt. But here was what was strange: how did the Yalta hoaxer know Woland, who had arrived in Moscow only yesterday? How did he know about the connection between Likhodeyev and Woland?
“‘By hypnosis...’” Varenukha kept repeating the word from the telegram. “How does he know about Woland?” He blinked and suddenly cried resolutely: “No, no, nonsense, nonsense, nonsense!”
“Where is he staying, this Woland, devil take him?” asked Rimsky.

Varenukha immediately got through to the Intourist bureau and, to Rimsky’s utter surprise, announced that Woland was staying in Likhodeyev’s apartment. After that, dialing the number of Likhodeyev’s apartment, Varenukha listened for a long time to the thick buzzing in the receiver. Amid the buzzing, from somewhere far away, a heavy, gloomy voice was heard singing: “...rocks, my refuge...”—and Varenukha decided that a voice from a radio play had broken into the telephone network from somewhere.
“The apartment doesn’t answer,” said Varenukha, putting the receiver back on the hook. “Maybe try calling again...”

He did not finish. The same woman appeared in the doorway again, and both of them, Rimsky and Varenukha, rose to meet her, and she took out of her pouch a sheet that was no longer white but somehow dark.
“This is getting interesting,” Varenukha said through his teeth, following the hurrying woman out with his eyes. Rimsky was the first to take possession of the sheet.
Against the dark background of the photographic paper, black handwritten lines stood out clearly:
“Proof my handwriting my signature Wire confirmation place Woland under secret surveillance Likhodeyev.”

In his twenty years of working in theaters Varenukha had seen all sorts of things, but now he felt that his mind was being clouded as if by a veil, and he could utter nothing except the commonplace and, moreover, completely absurd phrase:
“This cannot be!”
Rimsky acted differently. He got up, opened the door, and barked through it at the messenger woman sitting on a stool:
“Don’t let anyone in except postmen!” And he locked the door.

Then he took a stack of papers out of the desk and began carefully comparing the bold, left-slanting letters in the photogram with the letters in Styopa’s instructions on documents and in his signatures, which came with a corkscrew flourish. Varenukha, leaning his weight on the desk, breathed hotly on Rimsky’s cheek.
“It’s his handwriting,” the financial director said firmly at last, and Varenukha responded like an echo:
“His.”

Peering into Rimsky’s face, the house manager marveled at the change that had come over it. The financial director, thin enough already, seemed to have grown even thinner and even older, and his eyes in their horn-rimmed frames had lost their usual prickliness, and there had appeared in them not only alarm but even sadness.

Varenukha did everything that a man is supposed to do in moments of great astonishment. He ran around the office, and twice raised his arms like a man crucified, and drank a whole glass of yellowish water from the carafe, and exclaimed:
“I don’t understand! I don’t understand! I do-not-un-der-stand!”

Rimsky, though, was looking out of the window and thinking hard about something. The financial director’s position was a very difficult one. He needed, right then and there, without moving from the spot, to invent ordinary explanations for extraordinary phenomena.

Narrowing his eyes, the financial director pictured Styopa, in a nightshirt and without boots, climbing into some unheard-of super-high-speed airplane today at about half past eleven, and then the same Styopa, also at half past eleven, standing in his socks at the airfield in Yalta... The devil knows what this is!

Maybe it was not Styopa who had talked to him on the telephone today from his own apartment? No, it was Styopa talking! As if he didn’t know Styopa’s voice! And even if it had not been Styopa talking today, why, no later than yesterday, toward evening, Styopa had come from his own office into this very office with that idiotic contract and irritated the financial director with his frivolity. How could he have left by train or by air without saying anything at the theater? And even if he had flown off yesterday evening, he would not have arrived by noon today. Or would he?
“How many kilometers is it to Yalta?” asked Rimsky.
Varenukha stopped his running about and yelled:
“I’ve thought of it! Already thought of it! To Sevastopol by rail it’s about fifteen hundred kilometers. And to Yalta add another eighty kilometers. Well, by air it’s less, of course.”

Hm... Yes... Trains were out of the question. But what, then? A fighter plane? Who would let Styopa into a fighter plane without boots, and what fighter plane? What for? Maybe he took his boots off after flying into Yalta? Same thing: what for? And even in boots they wouldn’t let him into a fighter! And anyway, a fighter has nothing to do with it. It was written, after all, that he had turned up at the criminal investigation department at half past eleven in the morning, and he had been talking on the telephone in Moscow... just a moment... here the dial of his watch rose before Rimsky’s eyes... He was trying to remember where the hands had been. Horror! It had been at twenty past eleven. So what does that come to? If we suppose that instantly after the conversation Styopa rushed to the airfield and reached it in, say, five minutes, which, by the way, is also unthinkable, then it turns out that the plane, taking off right away, covered over a thousand kilometers in five minutes? Consequently, in an hour it covers more than twelve thousand kilometers!! That cannot be, and so he is not in Yalta.

What is left, then? Hypnosis? There is no such hypnosis in the world as could fling a man a thousand kilometers! So he is imagining that he is in Yalta? He may well be imagining it, but is the Yalta criminal investigation department imagining it too?! Oh no, excuse me, that does not happen!.. But they are telegraphing from there, aren’t they?

The financial director’s face was literally frightening. Meanwhile someone was turning and yanking the door handle from outside, and the messenger woman could be heard shouting desperately behind the door:
“You can’t! I won’t let you in! Not if you cut my throat! There’s a meeting!”
Rimsky took hold of himself as best he could, picked up the telephone receiver and said into it:
“Give me a top-priority call to Yalta.”
“Clever!” Varenukha exclaimed mentally.
But the call to Yalta did not take place. Rimsky put down the receiver and said:
“As luck would have it, the line is out of order.”

It was evident that the line’s being out of order had for some reason upset him especially badly and even made him thoughtful. After thinking a little, he again took up the receiver with one hand, and with the other began writing down what he was saying into it:

“Take an extra-urgent telegram. Variety. Yes. Yalta. Criminal investigation. Yes. ‘Today about half past eleven Likhodeyev spoke with me by telephone Moscow stop. After that did not come to work and cannot locate him by telephone stop. Confirm handwriting stop. Taking measures to watch said artiste. Financial director Rimsky.’”
“Very clever!” thought Varenukha, but before he had time to think it properly, the words flashed through his head: “Stupid! He can’t be in Yalta!”

Meanwhile Rimsky did the following: he neatly folded all the telegrams received and the copy of his own into a bundle, put the bundle into an envelope, sealed it, wrote a few words on it, and handed it to Varenukha, saying:
“Take it there right now, Ivan Savelyevich, in person. Let them sort it out there.”

“Now that really is clever!” thought Varenukha, and put the envelope away in his briefcase. Then, just in case, he dialed the number of Styopa’s apartment on the telephone once more, listened, and began winking and grimacing joyfully and mysteriously. Rimsky craned his neck.
“May I speak to the artiste Woland?” Varenukha asked sweetly.
“They are busy,” the receiver answered in a jangling voice. “And who is asking?”
“Varenukha, house manager of the Variety.”
“Ivan Savelyevich?” the receiver cried out joyfully. “Terribly glad to hear your voice! How is your health?”
“Merci,” Varenukha answered in amazement. “And who am I speaking to?”
“His assistant, his assistant and interpreter Koroviev,” the receiver rattled, “entirely at your service, dearest Ivan Savelyevich! Dispose of me as you please. So?”
“Excuse me, is Stepan Bogdanovich Likhodeyev not at home just now?”
“Alas, no! No!” the receiver shouted. “He’s gone out.”
“Where to?”
“Out of town, for a drive in the car.”
“Wh... what? A dr... drive?.. And when will he be back?”
“He said, I’ll get a breath of fresh air and come back!”
“I see...” Varenukha said in confusion. “Merci. Kindly tell Monsieur Woland that his performance tonight is in the third part.”
“Very good. Of course. Without fail. Urgently. Absolutely without fail. I’ll tell him,” the receiver rapped out abruptly.
“All the best,” Varenukha said in surprise.
“Please accept,” the receiver was saying, “my best, my warmest greetings and wishes! Success! Good luck! Perfect happiness! Everything!”
“Well, of course! What did I tell you!” the house manager shouted excitedly. “It’s not Yalta at all, he’s gone out of town!”
“Well, if that’s so,” the financial director began, turning pale with rage, “then it really is swinishness beyond words!”
Here the house manager jumped up and shouted so loudly that Rimsky started:
“I remember! I remember! A cheburek house called the Yalta has opened in Pushkino! It’s all clear! He went there, got drunk, and now he’s telegraphing from there!”

“Well, that’s going too far,” Rimsky answered, his cheek twitching, and real, heavy rage burned in his eyes. “Well, then, this outing is going to cost him dearly!..” He suddenly stumbled and added uncertainly: “But how can that be, the criminal investigation...”
“That’s nonsense! His own little jokes,” the effusive house manager interrupted, and asked: “And the packet—should I take it?”
“Without fail,” Rimsky answered.
And again the door opened, and in came that same... “Her!” Rimsky thought, for some reason with anguish. And they both rose to meet the postwoman.
This time the telegram contained the words:
“Thank you confirmation urgently five hundred criminal investigation for me tomorrow flying Moscow Likhodeyev.”
“He’s gone mad...” Varenukha said weakly.
Rimsky, however, jingled his key, took money out of a drawer of the fireproof safe, counted out five hundred rubles, rang, handed the money to the messenger and sent him to the telegraph office.
“For pity’s sake, Grigory Danilovich,” said Varenukha, not believing his eyes, “if you ask me, you’re sending that money for nothing.”
“It will come back,” Rimsky responded quietly, “but he’ll answer dearly for this little picnic.” And he added, pointing to Varenukha’s briefcase: “Off you go, Ivan Savelyevich, don’t delay.”
And Varenukha ran out of the office with the briefcase.

He went down to the ground floor, saw an enormously long line at the box office, learned from the cashier that she expected a full house within an hour, because the public had simply come pouring in as soon as they saw the supplementary poster, told the cashier to set aside and not sell thirty of the best seats in the boxes and the stalls, darted out of the box office, fought off the importunate free-pass seekers right there on the run, and dived into his own little office to grab his cap. At that moment the telephone rattled.
“Yes!” shouted Varenukha.
